policy: Agent C venue proposals for revision 1.201: strong and moderate only (Settler Colonial Studies, AICRJ, Wíčazo Ša Review, American Indian Quarterly, NAIS, Decolonization). Weak candidates (Native Studies Review, Canadian Journal of Native Studies) are held: their records are in new-journal-records.json without edges. Founded_for edges are in founding-batch shape; principal_venue edges must be routed as added_edges in a venue_correction batch (as founding-004/005/006). The 'strength' key is advisory and should be removed on acceptance. Community-controlled sources are not used.
fingerprint_note: Fingerprints of the two existing nodes computed from journal_catalogue in historiography-1920-2000.json (1.200) on 2026-10-27; recompute against the catalogue the batch is applied to. The four new journals need nodes first (new-journal-records.json); their ids follow build_journal_catalogue.stable_id('journal', normalized_title).

sources.title: Lorenzo Veracini, "Introducing settler colonial studies," Settler Colonial Studies 1:1 (2011): 1–12 (author's deposit)
sources.note: Inaugural editorial read in full in the period-4 wave (graph source p4b_veracini_2011_deposit): the journal 'aims to contribute to the consolidation of a new scholarly field' (p. 1); ARC Discovery funding (acknowledgements).

sources.title: Corey Snelgrove, Rita Kaur Dhamoon and Jeff Corntassel, "Unsettling Settler Colonialism," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3:2 (2014): 1–32
sources.note: Read in the period-4 wave (graph source screq_snelgrove_dhamoon_corntassel_2014): Settler Colonial Studies first published 2011 in open access and volunteer-run, moving to Taylor & Francis within two years (p. 9); Wolfe's paired 2013 special issues of Settler Colonial Studies 3:3 and AICRJ 37:2 (p. 10).

sources.note: Graph source p4b_goeman_2016 (period-4 wave): a memorial to Wolfe in AICRJ, attesting the journal's role in the settler-colonial exchange. URL as recorded there should be checked against the graph record before acceptance.

sources.title: UCLA American Indian Studies Center, About us and About AICRJ
sources.note: Read: the Center founded 1969 after students, faculty and community members pressed UCLA; AICRJ 'in print since 1971'; a multidisciplinary journal of Native American studies (self-description). Volume 1 under the present title is dated 1974 (Crossref).

Retrospective institutional account; co-founders named elsewhere not verified.

edges.relationship: Founded in 2011 by Lorenzo Veracini to contribute to the consolidation of settler colonial studies as a scholarly field; open access and volunteer-run at first, with Taylor & Francis from 2013.
edges.evidence_note: Veracini's inaugural editorial states the founding programme (p. 1); Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014, p. 9) record the open-access start and the move to Taylor & Francis. The journal follows Wolfe (1999, 2006); it dates a journal event, not the field's origin.

edges.relationship: Carried Wolfe's 2013 special issue 'The Settler Complex', paired with Settler Colonial Studies, and a 2016 memorial to him: a venue where settler-colonial theory met Native American studies.
edges.evidence_note: Snelgrove et al. 2014, p. 10 (the paired 2013 issues, SCS 3:3 and AICRJ 37:2); Williams 2016 cites Wolfe's 'The Settler Complex: An Introduction', AICRJ 37:2 (2013): 1–22; Goeman's 2016 memorial. AICRJ's longer role in Native American studies (AISC: in print since 1971) is not reviewed here.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the settler-colonial exchange only; an edge to `indigenous` for the journal's main role awaits a longitudinal source.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field's lifespan nor a publication start or cessation claim.

edges.relationship: Founded in 1985 at Eastern Washington University by Elizabeth Cook-Lynn as a journal for Indigenous peoples of the Americas to take possession of their own intellectual and creative pursuits; later carried Rigney (1999) and S. A. Miller (2009).
edges.evidence_note: The programme is stated in a 2025 institutional retrospective, not a 1985 editorial; co-founders are not verified. If 'a later launch mission alone is insufficient' is applied strictly, convert to principal_venue 1999–2009 on the Rigney and Miller articles. Target agreed with Agent B (part 2).

edges.relationship: Two issues carry the field's statements: in 1996 Wilson on tribal and family historians beside Mihesuah, S. A. Miller, Cook-Lynn and Champagne; in 2009 Innes on insider research and McCallum on Indigenous labour.
edges.evidence_note: Crossref contents of AIQ 20:1 (1996) and 33:4 (2009); Wilson 1996 pp. 3–5 read in full; Innes 2009 through Leddy 2010; Fixico 2009 opening read; other articles by title. The 1996 issue also serves `indigenous` (part 2).
edges.selection_note: A selected interval resting on two issues, not a survey of the journal; its founding (vol. 1, 1974) and sponsor are not verified.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field's lifespan nor a publication start or cessation claim.

edges.relationship: NAISA's journal from 2014 asks empirical studies to document approvals required by Native nations, tribes or bands, and especially encourages studies grounded in Indigenous research methodologies.
edges.evidence_note: NAISA journal page (current remit; founding co-editors O'Brien and Warrior, 2013–2019); Crossref vol. 1 (2014) and the 2021 editors' introduction on editorial ethics (title only). Not founded_for: the remit is current, not a dated founding statement.
edges.selection_note: Selected for its research-ethics and methodology remit; not a claim that every article belongs to the field.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field's lifespan nor a publication start or cessation claim. The remit was read on the current page.
